proposal.hypothesis: Li3PO4 is a wide-gap (~5 eV) electronic insulator with high oxidative stability, so it should resist decomposition at the 4.0 V LiCoO2 interface. Its Li-rich phosphate chemistry is close to the PS4 framework of Li6PS5Cl, so little interfacial reaction energy is expected. It is a standard, well-characterized coating family, which makes it a sound first probe of the penalty landscape.

LiF is a very wide-gap, electronically insulating fluoride with high oxidative stability at 4.0 V vs Li, so it should resist oxidation by LiCoO2. Its Li-F bonding is strongly ionic and it is generally chemically inert toward Li-rich sulfides, so it should avoid the P-O/sulfide oxidation pathway that gave the Li3PO4 penalty. It is a different chemical family from the phosphate probe, so it tests whether halide coatings reduce the interface penalty.
proposal.motivation: Li3PO4 (phosphate) gave penalty 0.337 eV/non-Li atom (bin 16, not acceptable) from interfacial decomposition to P2O5 and sulfur/chlorine products with Li6PS5Cl. A chemically different, fluoride-based coating is needed to test whether the penalty can drop below the 0.05 eV acceptance threshold.

proposal.hypothesis: Li2O is the most Li-rich candidate and contains only O2-, so it has no P, S, or F centers that could be reduced or oxidized in the way Li3PO4 and LiF were. Its wide gap (about 5 eV) should keep it electronically insulating. A Li-rich, low-valent oxide should be chemically compatible with the Li+-rich sulfide electrolyte. It tests whether a simple oxide family lowers the contact penalty below the roughly 0.3 eV seen for the phosphate and fluoride probes.

Li3PO4 and LiF both gave penalties of about 0.3 eV, so an Al-based oxide is a chemically distinct probe of whether the contact penalty can be reduced.
